title: Securing and Respecting Users’ Privacy
subtitle: Design collection, consent, retention, and deletion around user expectations
summary: Pip opens the town’s search logs and finds private worries, not harmless keywords. Removing names will not make the records safe. Residents help define collection, consent, retention, and deletion; Pip learns that privacy is a promise people experience, with limits that the architecture must make clear.

concepts.title: Privacy pillars
concepts.body: Pip proudly opens the search dashboard. A resident asks, “You kept that?” Privacy means no surprises, transparency, meaningful consent, and control—not merely a protected database. Pip explains collection before it starts, offers meaningful choices, and makes the retention period visible. The experience must match the promise.

steps.text: Protection is not only a database property.
Explain collection and offer meaningful control.

concepts.title: Data minimization
concepts.body: Pip adds a birth-date field to the town’s delivery form for possible future marketing. A resident asks why delivering a parcel requires it. Data minimization collects only what the stated purpose needs. Pip removes the field: less exposure and breach impact, but fewer personalization and analysis possibilities. “Just in case” is not a purpose.

steps.text: Pip asks what delivery actually needs.
An address serves the stated purpose.
Collect less, accepting the analytics trade-off.

concepts.title: Retention and deletion
concepts.body: A resident deletes a search history; Pip finds a replica still holding it. Retention means keeping data only as long as necessary and communicating that period. Control includes deletion and applicable erasure rights. Pip follows copies, backups, and derived data, documenting removal timing instead of promising an instant disappearance the system cannot deliver.

steps.text: The live record is only one copy.

concepts.title: Anonymization limits
concepts.body: Pip removes names from a town dataset, then recognizes a resident through precise times and locations. Generalization and k-anonymity reduce uniqueness, not every re-identification risk; the book’s Netflix case illustrates auxiliary information’s power. Differential privacy uses carefully calibrated noise for broader protection. Pip reviews the release rather than declaring unnamed records anonymous.

misconceptions.claim: Privacy pillars is equivalent to ordinary functional correctness.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter separates this concern from “works as coded”: From a user perspective privacy means no surprises, transparency, meaningful consent, and control.

misconceptions.claim: A single review proves the product will remain responsible.
misconceptions.correction: Users, contexts, and dependencies change; feedback, monitoring, and revision are required.

scenario.title: Retention for workplace search
scenario.context: Pip’s town-services search retains queries to improve ranking. Searches reveal health and personal concerns; residents never expected a lasting record.

options.label: Minimize and expire queries transparently
options.benefit: Residents understand collection and control; less retained data limits exposure.
options.consequence: Pip explains retention and removes raw queries on schedule.

options.label: Keep indefinite raw history
options.cost: Sensitive concerns become visible to a broad internal audience.
options.consequence: Residents discover the unexpected record; the team must explain and remove it.

scenario.debrief: Pip must justify collection and retention to the people affected. Convenience does not erase privacy obligations or re-identification risk.

quiz.question: Which is a user-facing privacy pillar?
quiz.explanation: The chapter names no surprises, transparency, consent, and control.

quiz.question: What does data minimization mean?
options: Collect only information necessary for the stated purpose.
Collect everything in case it becomes useful.
Delete the user interface after collection.
quiz.explanation: Minimization reduces exposure by limiting collection to a need.

quiz.question: Why is k-anonymity not an absolute privacy guarantee?
options: Auxiliary information can re-identify records even when direct identifiers are removed.
quiz.explanation: The Netflix example illustrates re-identification from supposedly anonymized data.

exercise.title: Design privacy controls
exercise.prompt: Choose collected data and its purpose.
